Olney
OHL-nee
n. (the Buckinghamshire lace town where John Newton was curate and where he and William Cowper produced the Olney Hymns of 1779)
Old English Ollaneg, Olla's island or water-meadow, from a personal name and eg, an island.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Olney is the small lace-making town on the Ouse in north Buckinghamshire, and it is one of the few English villages whose name belongs to the history of worship. John Newton, who had been master of a slave ship and was converted at sea and then over years of reading, was ordained in 1764 and came to Olney as curate, where he stayed sixteen years. He preached to lacemakers and labourers, kept a weekly meeting for children, and wrote a hymn for most of his prayer meetings so that the congregation might sing what had just been preached. William Cowper, the poet, came to live in the town in 1767 and became Newton's friend and collaborator despite the recurring derangement that overshadowed his life. Their joint collection, the Olney Hymns, was published in 1779 with three hundred and forty-eight pieces, Newton writing the greater number, including the hymn beginning Amazing grace, and Cowper contributing sixty-eight, among them God moves in a mysterious way and There is a fountain filled with blood. The dictionary records the book as the plainest English demonstration that doctrine put into verse and sung by a congregation will outlive the sermons it came from.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song of adoration to God; grace as the free unmerited favour of God; a fountain as a spring; to guide as to lead; and to shine as to emit light.

expand to see more

HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; among pagans, a poem in honour of a deity; a sacred lyric.

GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God; the divine influence which renews the heart and restrains from sin.

FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; the source or first principle of anything.

GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path; to influence or direct.

SHINE, v.i. To emit rays of light; to give light; to be bright; to be lively or animated.

Key Scripture

Mal 4:2 — "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall."

Pro 4:18 — "But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day."

Luk 1:79 — "To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace."

Act 26:18 — "To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me."

Modern Corruption

Buckinghamshire lace town where John Newton was curate for sixteen years from 1764 and where he and William Cowper produced the Olney Hymns of 1779, three hundred and forty-eight pieces in all.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a hymn is a vehicle for doctrine and is answerable to doctrine, not a vehicle for feeling that happens to use religious words. Newton wrote for a particular prayer meeting on a particular text so that his lacemakers would carry the week's teaching home in a form they could not easily lose; the hymns are therefore full of the substance of the faith, ruin, grace, imputation, perseverance, and they name it. The figure Newton reached for most often is the one Scripture itself uses for the arrival of mercy on a blind man, and the apostolic commission states it as the purpose of preaching: “To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18).

The second thing to recover is Cowper, and here the dictionary speaks against a sentimentality that would smooth him out. Cowper believed for long stretches that he himself was lost, attempted his own life, and wrote some of the best hymns in the language out of that darkness; his collaborator was a converted slaver who never stopped calling himself a wretch. Neither man is evidence that assurance is easy, and the hymns are not cheerful. What they hold to is a dawn promised rather than felt: “unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (Mal 4:2), and a path that brightens by degrees rather than at once, since “the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18). Zacharias had sung the same thing of men still sitting in the dark, that God would “give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luk 1:79). Olney produced that book out of a curacy among lacemakers, and the dictionary counts it among the most fruitful sixteen years any English parish ever had.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness; Hebrew nogah (H5051), brightness; Greek anoigo (G455), to open.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness, rightness; “shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings”, Malachi 4:2.

Hebrew 'or (H216) — light, daylight; “the path of the just is as the shining light”, Proverbs 4:18.

Greek epiphaino (G2014) — to shine upon, to appear; “To give light to them that sit in darkness”, Luke 1:79.

Greek anoigo (G455) — to open; “To open their eyes”, Acts 26:18.

Greek aphesis (G859) — a release, forgiveness, remission; “that they may receive forgiveness of sins”, Acts 26:18.

Usage

"“To open their eyes” (Act 26:18) — the figure Newton reached for most often."

"“shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18) — a dawn promised rather than felt."

"“to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luk 1:79) — Cowper writing out of his own darkness."
